##### **Transcript**

Hello again, back in Riyadh again this week, was in Abu Dhabi briefly on on Friday, but now back in the Kingdom and one of the things about working on matters here at the moment. Is. Sort of. The scope and complexity of projects and the forms of contract being used are revolving, and there's an awful lot of. Issues around that, I wanted to talk about two things which are relatively common themes in projects in the Kingdom at the moment that I've been dealing with already today. And the first one really is about the government Procurement law. Now of course, you know, the government Procurement law has been amended and updated, albeit recently I think 2019, but there's also a much earlier version of that law and that applies to contracts entered into by government. Agencies. Now many of the GIGA projects are not structured as those agencies and so fall outside the government procurement law. But there are still many projects which fall within the government procurement law. And a common area of debate is between contractors and owners about the capacity to claim for change and the government procurement law. In both versions. Both the older version and the current version provides under Article 69. A capacity for the government agency to increase the work, so issue change orders for up to 10% of the contract value and to decrease the scope for up to 20% of the contract value. And a number of issues arise out of this, and I just want to address them briefly because there's something I've been dealing with. As I say, right now, the contractors rely on the operation of the government procurement law effectively as a contractual argument. And so they say that you have a power to increase the scope by 10%, but over that then we are entitled to, for example, modify our pricing basis of rates. And if it's a bill of quantity schedule of rates type arrangement because it's gone beyond the 10% and vice versa in relation to the 20%. So you've reduced it by 20%, we get to change our rates, you increase it over 10%, we get to change our rates. Article 69 of the procurement will really operates just to limit the power of the government agency without having to go back to the Ministry of Finance to make a change. Nowhere in it or indeed even in the. Regulations which are also issued underneath. Does it talk about anything other really than than that? But contractors have made the argument and continue to to make the argument that if it goes up by more than 10%, you don't have the power to issue that change as a function of the procurement law. And so as a consequence, I get to change my rates moving forward generally because over 110%. Of course, this is based on the sort of general or position that is commonly held in. In many jurisdictions that the ability to issue change orders beyond a certain value changes the nature of the contract and as a result the the rates can't apply to that contract. The difference in Saudi Arabia is that a 10% cap under the procurement law and a 20% reduction. So cap increase reduction reduction really probably doesn't get you to the same place that you would expect it to in terms of other jurisdictions. So if you look at English law position, a 10% increase in the overall scope wouldn't necessarily. Say it may, but as a general rule wouldn't invalidate the underlying pricing basis of the contract such that the deal itself had changed and the contractor could have escaped the rates and and so. The contractors position that this is a 10% under the Saudi procurement law is perhaps curious because certainly on on its face, the reading of the law provides that the 10% cap is really in regulation for the agency before it needs to go back and get Ministry of Finance approval and modify the sums payable. Not necessarily a vehicle through which the contractor can make a claim. They really need to look at their underlying contract to see if they can make a claim. And yet that issue is one that's sort of. Constantly are being raised here. The second point. And so I would think if we're in a common law jurisdiction, 1 view of it would be well, no, that's, that's a a functional administrative limitation. It might be helpful, but I don't think it by itself gets you to change your rates. I think actually you probably need to change your rates if it's more substantial of the nature of the contract itself changes. So we're looking at 2030% or 10% that is materially different. So something completely out with the intended scope. Second argument I see deployed a lot is the argument that the 10% applies to individual items rather than to. The overall scope, well, that's just not what Article 69 says. And I don't think a 10% increase in an individual item, which doesn't represent a 10% overall increase, could be said to fit within that. Now obviously the Arabic version governs and there is some. Differences perhaps in drafting of the English version of the Arabic version, but I'm not sure the Arabic version gets there either. And I do think that on balance the position on procurement law is it's a vehicle to regulate and control the government agencies spending and behaviour rather than anything else, and to provide for legal stopgaps. The better argument the contractor has is that an increase over 10% is beyond legal power and as a consequence changes the contract in a way that would entitle them to. To apply for separate rates because the contract itself as a function of of, of law, because it is a law is different now. And that's why that law is there now. That argument is, you know, played out and it's going on lots of projects at the moment where the governments involved directly. And that's quite an interesting argument to look at. I think we have to step back and be sort of thoughtful about the, the purpose of the legislation, the vehicle through which it operates and the change itself in order to see whether it applies. But ultimately does come back to the contract and how the contract deals with rates rather than relying solely on the procurement law. The other thing that seems to be a theme at the moment is that there's an awful lot of works going on principally hearing Riyadh that I'm I'm talking about today where the contractor. That has. Effectively a schedule of rates for valuing works and they're paid on progress basis and that's a pretty well understood and well trodden position. The contracts provide the usual thing that you have to identify. Any errors in in the tender documents during tender period and notify otherwise and if you don't, it's deemed included in your prices. But a reasonably common theme that we see occurring relates to changes. In the actual. So, so differences between say the drawings which provide material specification and specifications and the bill of quantities and the bill of quantities itself identifies certain things. But one of the things that has been a theme because there's so much happening so quickly is the drawings identifying certain materials being used which are not then specified in the bill of quantities at all. And the owners of position under the contract tends to be, well, look, if it's not in the bill of quantities, but it is in the drawings and you do give this warranty. Into the contract terms itself that anything not specifically. Included is is deemed included in the rates and built into existing rates and this is a an item of work for which you won't get recovery. And that actually technically is a matter of Salvador is possible that certainly in good faith to operate it that way absent any other circumstances. But where it becomes a material change. We've seen quite a few of them here where there is something which is there were wasn't provided for it all and was, you know, in the 10s of billions of of work. It's difficult to adopt A formalistic approach and expect it to be consistent with with good faith, although good faith is clear. I would certainly. The starting off point has to be that if the contract provides for. The fact that if it's not specified, then it's included in the rates and it wasn't specified and there was opportunity for them to do the things they need to do during tender period. There's an opportunity for them to ask questions. They ask questions. They didn't ask questions about this. Then the starting place has to be that it's included and there need to be some pretty powerful reasons as to why not. A lot of that's practical though. People make mistakes and it could be the case that it was a mistake, although it could equally be that it's already built into the rates and would be a an extra profit if it wasn't. But that's kind of going on a lot at the moment because of the the race to get projects out, the fact that many projects have very extensive technical schedules put together in a hurry and things get missed. Drawings which usually rate higher priority obviously to be Q and the BOQ themselves. But the sorts of issues that are coming up on a day-to-day basis here in Riyadh are really fascinating for construction practitioners because they are all of the things you would expect to see with a layer of, you know, effectively foreign law on top complexity and novel issues being thrown up every day. It's a wonderful place for construction lawyers at the moment. I hope that's helpful. And I'll talk to you all soon. Thank you.

Sometimes in lump sum contracts, sometimes to stay competitive, the contractor takes a loss in one item only to cover that loss onto another item, hoping a future addition of the profitable item. These variations take a bad turn, when the contract is lump sum, and the profitable items get deleted. Quite risky for the contractor.   💡 Why do so many contractors collapse in Africa, even when they are technically excellent? It’s not always poor workmanship. This principle — often called “Pay Now, Argue Later” — keeps projects alive. Across Africa, two major frameworks make this possible: 1️⃣ Statutory Adjudication (Kenya’s 2025 Bills) Fast-track decisions (within weeks, not years). Prevents disputes from choking progress. When used properly, both systems are lifelines. I’ve witnessed projects in Guinea, Kenya, and beyond where adjudication literally saved hundreds of jobs by unlocking stalled payments.   Many professionals in the construction industry often confuse three key terms: 1-Contract Type 2-Contract Form 3-Procurement Pathway Although they may appear similar, each plays a distinct role in the project life cycle. 1-Procurement Pathway It is the route that determines who designs and who builds the project in other words, the method by which the stages of design, construction, and supply are managed. Examples of procurement pathways: • Traditional (Design–Bid–Build) • Design & Build • Management Contracting 2-Contract Type It defines how risks and costs are distributed between the contracting parties — in other words, the payment mechanism and financial responsibility during the execution of the project. Examples of contract types: • Lump Sum / Fixed Price Contract • Unit Rate / Measurement Contract • Cost Plus Contract 3-Contract Form It is the legal document that governs the relationship between the parties, defining their rights, obligations, and contractual procedures, such as variations, claims, and dispute resolution. Examples of contract forms: • FIDIC (International Standard Form) • NEC (New Engineering Contract) • Omani Standard Form of Contract for Construction (2019) Think of it as a journey: • The Pathway is the map that defines the route from start to finish. • The Type is the driving rule that determines who bears the fuel and risks. • The Form is the official contract that sets out the legal and administrative framework for the trip.
